lessons.title: La paire de chaussures
lessons.text:
Il était une fois une paire de chaussures qui étaient mariées ensemble. La chaussure droite, qui était le monsieur, s'appelait Nicolas, et la chaussure gauche, qui était la dame, s'appelait Tina.

Elles habitaient une belle boîte en carton où elles étaient roulées dans du papier de soie. Elles s'y trouvaient parfaitement heureuses, et elles espéraient bien que cela durerait toujours.

Mais voilà qu'un beau matin une vendeuse les sortit de leur boîte afin de les essayer à une dame. La dame les mit, fit quelques pas avec, puis, voyant qu'elles lui allaient bien, elle dit :
— Je les achète.
— Faut-il vous les envelopper ? demanda la vendeuse.
— Inutile, dit la dame, je rentre avec.
Elle paya et sortit, avec les chaussures neuves aux pieds.

C'est ainsi que Nicolas et Tina marchèrent toute une journée sans se voir l'un l'autre. Le soir seulement ils se retrouvèrent dans un placard obscur.
— C'est toi, Tina ?
— Oui, c'est moi, Nicolas.
— Ah, quel bonheur ! Je te croyais perdue !
— Moi aussi. Mais où étais-tu ?
— Moi ? J'étais au pied droit.
— Moi, j'étais au pied gauche.
— Je comprends tout, dit Nicolas. Toutes les fois que tu étais en avant, moi, j'étais en arrière, et lorsque tu étais en arrière, moi, j'étais en avant. C'est pour cela que nous ne pouvions pas nous voir.
— Et cette vie-là va recommencer chaque jour ? demanda Tina.
— Je le crains !
— Mais c'est affreux ! Rester toute la journée sans te voir, mon petit Nicolas ! Je ne pourrai jamais m'y habituer !
— Écoute, dit Nicolas, j'ai une idée : Puisque je suis toujours à droite et toi toujours à gauche, eh bien, chaque fois que j'avancerai, je ferai en même temps un petit écart de ton côté. Comme ça, nous nous dirons bonjour. D'accord ?
— D'accord !

Ainsi fit Nicolas, de sorte que, tout au long du jour suivant, la dame qui portait les chaussures ne pouvait plus faire trois pas sans que son pied droit vienne accrocher son talon gauche, et plaf ! à chaque fois, elle s'étalait par terre.

Très inquiète, elle alla, le jour même, consulter un médecin.
— Docteur, je ne sais pas ce que j'ai. Je me fais des croche-pieds à moi-même !
— Des croche-pieds à vous-même ?
— Oui, docteur ! À chaque pas que je fais, ou presque, mon pied droit accroche mon talon gauche, et cela me fait tomber !
— C'est très grave, dit le docteur. Si cela continue, il faudra vous couper le pied droit. Tenez, voici une ordonnance : vous en avez pour dix mille francs de médicaments. Donnez-moi deux mille francs pour la consultation, et revenez me voir demain.

Le soir même, dans le placard, Tina demandait à Nicolas :
— Tu as entendu ce qu'a dit le docteur ?
— Oui, j'ai entendu.
— C'est affreux ! Si on coupe le pied droit de la dame, elle te jettera, et nous serons séparés pour toujours ! Il faut faire quelque chose !
— Oui, mais quoi ?
— Écoute, j'ai une idée : puisque je suis à gauche, c'est moi, demain, qui ferai un petit écart à droite, à chaque fois que j'avancerai ! D'accord ?
— D'accord !

Ainsi fit-elle, de sorte que, tout au long du deuxième jour, c'était le pied gauche qui accrochait le talon droit, et plaf ! la pauvre dame se retrouvait par terre.

De plus en plus inquiète, elle retourna chez son médecin.
— Docteur, cela va de moins en moins ! Maintenant, c'est mon pied gauche qui accroche mon talon droit !
— C'est de plus en plus grave, dit le docteur. Si cela continue, il faudra vous couper les deux pieds ! Tenez, voici une ordonnance : vous en avez pour vingt mille francs de médicaments. Donnez-moi trois mille francs pour la consultation, et surtout, n'oubliez pas de revenir me voir demain !

Le soir même, Nicolas demandait à Tina :
— Tu as entendu ?
— J'ai entendu.
— Si l'on coupe les deux pieds de la dame, qu'allons-nous devenir ?
— Je n'ose pas y penser !
— Et pourtant, je t'aime, Tina !
— Moi aussi, Nicolas, je t'aime !
— Je voudrais ne jamais te quitter !
— Moi aussi, je le voudrais !

Ils parlaient ainsi, dans l'obscurité, sans se douter que la dame qui les avait achetés se promenait dans le couloir, en pantoufles, parce que les paroles du médecin l'empêchaient de dormir. En passant devant la porte du placard, elle entendit toute cette conversation et, comme elle était très intelligente, elle comprit tout.
« C'est donc ça, pensa-t-elle. Ce n'est pas moi qui suis malade, ce sont mes chaussures qui s'aiment ! Comme c'est gentil ! »

Là-dessus, elle jeta à la boîte aux ordures les trente mille francs de médicaments qu'elle avait achetés et le lendemain elle dit à sa femme de ménage :
— Vous voyez cette paire de chaussures ? Je ne les mettrai plus, mais je veux les garder quand même. Alors cirez-les bien, entretenez-les bien, qu'elles soient toujours brillantes, et surtout ne les séparez jamais l'une de l'autre !

Restée seule, la femme de ménage se dit :
« Madame est folle, de garder ces chaussures sans les mettre ! Dans une quinzaine de jours, quand Madame les aura oubliées, je les volerai ! »

Quinze jours plus tard, elle les vola et se les mit aux pieds. Mais quand elle les eut mises, elle aussi commença à se faire des croche-pieds à elle-même. Un soir, dans l'escalier de service, comme elle descendait les ordures, Nicolas et Tina voulurent s'embrasser, et badaboum ! Vlang ! Bing ! la femme de ménage se retrouva assise sur un palier, avec plein d'épluchures sur la tête, et une pelure de pomme de terre qui pendait, en spirale, sur son front, comme une boucle de cheveux.
« Ces chaussures sont sorcières, pensa-t-elle. Je ne les mettrai plus. Je vais les donner à ma nièce, qui est boiteuse ! »

C'est ce qu'elle fit. La nièce, qui était boiteuse, en effet, passait presque toute la journée assise sur une chaise, les pieds joints. Quand par hasard elle marchait, c'était si lentement qu'elle ne pouvait guère s'accrocher les pieds. Et les chaussures étaient heureuses car, même dans la journée, elles étaient le plus souvent côte à côte.

Cela dura longtemps. Malheureusement, comme la nièce était boiteuse, elle usait d'un côté plus vite que de l'autre.
Un soir, Tina dit à Nicolas :
— Je sens ma semelle qui devient fine, fine ! Je vais bientôt être percée !
— Ne fais pas ça ! dit Nicolas. Si on nous jette, nous allons être encore séparés !
— Je le sais bien, dit Tina, mais que faire ? Je ne peux pas m'empêcher de vieillir !

Et en effet, huit jours plus tard, sa semelle était trouée. La boiteuse acheta des chaussures neuves, et jeta Nicolas et Tina dans la boîte à ordures.
— Qu'allons-nous devenir ? demanda Nicolas.
— Je ne sais pas, dit Tina. Si seulement j'étais sûre de ne jamais te quitter !
— Approche-toi, dit Nicolas, et prends ma bride avec la tienne. De cette façon, nous ne serons pas séparés.
Ainsi firent-ils. Ensemble ils furent jetés à la poubelle, ensemble ils furent emportés par le camion des éboueurs, et abandonnés dans un terrain vague. Ils y restèrent ensemble jusqu'au jour où un petit garçon et une petite fille les y trouvèrent.
— Oh, regarde ! Les chaussures ! Elles sont bras dessus bras dessous !
— C'est qu'elles sont mariées ensemble, dit la petite fille.
— Eh bien, dit le petit garçon, puisqu'elles sont mariées ensemble, elles vont faire leur voyage de noces !

Le petit garçon prit les chaussures, les cloua côte à côte sur une planche, puis il porta la planche au bord de l'eau et la laissa descendre, au fil du courant, vers la mer. Pendant qu'elle s'éloignait, la petite fille agitait son mouchoir en criant :
— Adieu, chaussures, et bon voyage !

C'est ainsi que Nicolas et Tina, qui n'attendaient plus rien de l'existence, eurent quand même un beau voyage de noces.

lessons.title: La paire de chaussures : une histoire d’amour originale
lessons.text:
Le conte « La paire de chaussures » a été écrit par Pierre Gripari. Il fait partie du livre La sorcière de la rue Mouffetard et autres contes de la rue Broca. C’est un conte humoristique et fantastique. Les personnages principaux sont Nicolas, la chaussure droite, et Tina, la chaussure gauche.
Au début, Nicolas et Tina vivaient heureux dans une boîte. Mais un jour, une dame les a achetés et les a portés. Les chaussures ne pouvaient plus se voir, alors Nicolas a décidé de faire de petits mouvements pour rencontrer Tina. La dame est tombée plusieurs fois et elle a consulté un médecin. Heureusement, elle a compris que les chaussures s’aimaient. Plus tard, une femme de ménage les a volés, puis les a donnés à sa nièce. Finalement, les chaussures ont été jetées à la poubelle. Deux enfants les ont trouvées et leur ont offert un voyage de noces.
L’histoire est drôle et surprenante parce que les chaussures étaient amoureuses et pouvaient parler. Avant leur séparation, elles avaient toujours vécu ensemble. Le conflit principal était leur difficulté à rester ensemble.
Pour adapter ce conte, je choisirais un court-métrage d’animation pour enfants. Je garderais les personnages et les événements principaux, mais j’ajouterais des couleurs, de la musique et des dialogues amusants. Les chaussures pourraient avoir des yeux et des expressions pour montrer leurs émotions. Cette adaptation serait plus visuelle et amusante pour les enfants.
Je recommande ce conte aux enfants et aux personnes qui aiment les histoires originales. Il montre que l’amour et la fidélité sont importants. La fin est surprenante et touchante.

lessons.title: A phylogeny of extant penguins (Aves: Sphenisciformes) combining morphology and
lessons.text:
Abstract
The phylogenetic relationships among the penguins have received little attention, despite their well-known anatomy and the conspicuous nature of the group. Previous attempts have included datasets limited to few, mostly osteological characters, and one study was based on integumentary and breeding characters. We developed a morphological matrix comprising 159 morphological characters of osteology (70 characters), myology (15), digestive tract (1), integument (66), and breeding (7 characters), scored in 18 extant forms (all currently recognized species plus one distinct subspecies). A gaviiform was placed at the root, and 11 species of representative procellariiform groups completed the outgroup. A heuristic parsimony analysis under equal weights was performed.
We also compiled DNA sequences available in GenBank for the mitochondrial genes 12S rDNA and cytochrome b. We included  the two data partitions in a combined analysis under direct optimization. Both analyses recovered the monophyly of Sphenisciformes and all the traditional polytypic genera. Morphological characters performed optimally at the ordinal and generic nodes, also providing resolution and varying degrees of support at supra- and intrageneric nodes. The comparison of molecular and morphological results indicated that the most significant problem in the phylogeny of extant penguins is rooting the ingroup. The mutual interaction of molecular and morphological data decreases the ambiguity regarding the placement of the root, and provides a resolved, relatively well-supported phylogeny of extant penguins. Biogeographical patterns based on breeding ranges and derived from the combined analysis show that the major intercontinental vicariance events detected are consistent with cold marine current patterns of the Southern Hemisphere.

lessons.title: Comparison of paralog identification methods and their impact on species tree to
lessons.text: Target capture is a common method of generating high throughput DNA sequencing data for phylogenetic reconstruction of species relationships, for which single copy genes are usually most informative. However, a pervasive problem with target capture is that putatively single copy genes may in fact be paralogs resulting from gene duplication, which are problematic for phylogenetic inference because their evolutionary history may differ from the divergence history of species. Here, we use as a case study a target enrichment dataset of 88 species of Detarioideae (Leguminosae) with a focus on the Sindora clade to examine approaches for handling paralogs, including the built-in paralog handling functions in HybPiper and CAPTUS, plus subsequent steps using Putative Paralog Detection and the tree-based Yang & Smith orthology inference approach. We compare the paralogs flagged using these methods and verify their performance with BLAST mapping against a reference genome sequence of Sindora glabra, and then subsequently compare the species tree topologies produced across these methods. Our comparisons of paralogs flagged across the Sindora clade show that the Putative Paralog Detection pipeline was the most accurate in identifying paralogs in terms of its similarity to the BLAST mapping, followed by the built-in paralog identification function of CAPTUS. However, the results we recovered for the Detarioideae subfamily suggest that the largest differences in species tree topology resulted from the use of paralog-filtered alignments (such as with the Putative Paralog Detection pipeline and the Yang & Smith orthology inference approaches) rather than just by removing the sequences of identified paralogous genes. This was the true for HybPiper-assembled datasets but was not seen in CAPTUS-assembled datasets. In all comparisons, the topological differences caused by different paralog handling methods tended to be confined to clades where processes such as hybridisation and introgression are prevalent. Our study provides a roadmap to establish the best approach to identify, eliminate or separate paralogs in the absence of a chromosomally contiguous reference genome for a study group, and highlights the importance of careful data inspection and processing in addition to under-standing the extent of paralogy and paralog characteristics (e.g. sequence divergence between copies) for their study group.

Champe and Seymour Benzer Department of Biological Sciences, Purdue University, Lafayette, Indiana --- Summary An unusual rII mutant of phage T4 is described, in which a terminal portion of a cistron has been deleted without impairing the function of the remaining fragment. This suggests that the deleted section is non-essential. Nevertheless, mutations within this segment which do impair the function can be observed. --- 1. Introduction The entire amino acid sequence of an enzyme is not always essential to its function; a fragment of the molecule may retain all or part of the catalytic activity as shown, for example, by the work of Hill & Smith (1956) on papain, and Kalnitsky & Rogers (1956) on ribonuclease. Assuming that the amino acid sequence of an enzyme is dictated by the nucleotide sequence in a genetic structure, one might expect that it would be possible, in some instances, to delete a part of the genetic structure without seriously impairing the activity of its product. The present paper describes a mutant of bacteriophage T4 which appears to represent such a case. In this mutant, although a sizable fraction of the B cistron of the rII region has been deleted, the remaining fragment retains the B cistron function. 2. Results (a) The two cistrons in the rII region of phage T4 rII mutations in phage T4 prevent the phage from multiplying in strain K of E. coli. If a cell is also infected with the standard type phage, the function or functions needed by the mutant are supplied, and both mutant and standard type progeny are produced. Thus rII mutations are recessive. rII mutants can be classified into either of two functional groups by means of the cis-trans test (Benzer 1955, 1957), these groups being consistent with the location of the mutations either to the left or to the right of a unique divide in the genetic map constructed by recombination experiments. Of some hundreds of extended ("deletion") mutations that have been mapped in the rII region, four (r1605, rNB7006, r1231, and r1589) span the divide between the A and B cistrons, leaving fragments of a cistron on either side. A genetic map showing these mutations (and others pertinent to the following discussion) is given in Fig. 1. r1605, rNB7006, and r1231 behave in complementation tests in the expected way, that is, they fail to complement any A or B cistron mutant. However, the behavior of r1589 is exceptional. (b) Properties of the exceptional mutant r1589 The lesion in r1589 encompasses a large part of the A cistron and extends over 21 known sites (out of 129) of the B cistron. That is to say, when r1589 is crossed with any mutant located within or overlapping this span, no standard type recombinants have ever been detected in as many as 10^8 progeny. By the method of shrinkage of distance between outside markers (Nomura & Benzer, 1961) the lesion in r1589 has been shown (Bode, 1962) to be a true deletion. Now r1589, in spite of the fact that a sizable portion of the B cistron is missing, complements strongly every B cistron mutant with which it has been tested, including ones with overlapping extended mutations, such as r638. The phage yields per infected cell due to complementation are comparable to the standard type phage. r1589 does not, however, complement any A cistron mutant so far tested. Data for various combinations are given in Fig. 2. r1589 functions as if its B cistron (but not its A cistron) were intact. Thus, the portion of the B cistron deleted in r1589 appears to be non-essential for the activity of the remaining fragment. In mixed infection of K together with any B cistron mutant, r1589 supplies this active B fragment and the A activity is supplied by the other mutant, so that both necessary functions are present. Were it not for the fact that r1589 also has part of its lesion affecting the A cistron, it might not have appeared to be a mutant at all. This confronts us with a paradox. Mutations have been detected in the non-essential portion of the B cistron at at least 21 different sites, and these mutants lack B cistron activity. This suggests that mutations occurring in a non-essential portion may nevertheless prevent the expression of the remainder of the cistron. For instance, an alteration of the nucleotide sequence such that the information becomes "nonsense" could interfere with the completion of a polypeptide chain. The special properties of r1589 have been exploited by Crick, et al. (1961) in a brilliant experiment. They have shown that the B cistron function of r1589 can be eliminated by inserting certain deficiencies in its A cistron fragment, while other deficiencies have no effect. Their interpretation, reinforced by an impressive series of other experiments with suppressor mutations, is that deficiencies corresponding to an integral number of amino acid-determining groups (nucleotide triplets) allow continued formation of a polypeptide chain while non-integral deficiencies do not. It would appear that the lesion of r1589 represents an instance where the joining of the remaining A and B cistron fragments is such that the continuity of the information is not interrupted. It is to be noted that the mutations observable within the B-cistron span of r1589 include ones which are inducible to revert by the base analog 2-aminopurine, and therefore are probably due to substitutions of one base for another (Freese, 1959). Of the 21 known sites covered by r1589, eight are of this type, designated by asterisks in Fig. 1. This would seem to indicate that the genetic code is such that base pair substitutions are capable of converting sense to nonsense. In other words, the genetic code is not completely degenerate; not every triplet necessarily corresponds to an amino acid. Another possibility, however, is that certain amino acid substitutions, even in the non-essential region, could have drastic effects upon the folding of the rest of the polypeptide chain. 3. Discussion In the standard type phage, the A and B cistrons function as independent units. Presumably, there is some information element between the two cistrons that acts as a continuity break in the transcription of the genetic information. In r1589 this element must be missing and fortuitous joining of the A and B cistron fragments enables continuity to be preserved. The deletion r1231, which has also been shown by Bode (1962) to be a true deletion, extends only slightly further (2 known sites) into the B cistron than does r1589. However, r1231 lacks B cistron activity, as do rNB7006 and r1605 which extend still further. The loss of the B cistron activity of r1231 could be due to essentiality of the additional tiny segment involved, or to a non-fortuitous joining of the A and B fragments. In the latter case one would anticipate that insertion of suitable deletions to the left of r1231 according to Crick, et al., might revive its B cistron activity. r1589 is an illustration of how two cistrons can become joined together. One can easily imagine how the converse might also occur, i.e., the separation of one cistron into two parts, by a mutation which generates a continuity break at a suitable point. An example of an enzyme for which such cistron splitting could occur without deleterious effect is ribonuclease, since, as Richards (1958) has shown, the polypeptide chain can be cleaved into two fragments which, when both are present, still form an active enzyme. Genetically, this would then resemble the case of tryptophan synthetase in E. coli (Crawford & Yanofsky, 1958; Yanofsky & Crawford, 1959) where two dissociable chains of the enzyme are indeed controlled by two contiguous cistrons. lessons.title: React Ecosystem
lessons.text:
This is not a tutorial. It is a **forensic study guide for a senior frontend interview** — the kind where "senior" is measured not by years of `useState` muscle memory, but by the ability to defend architectural decisions, spot latent bugs in "working" code, and articulate why the obvious answer is often the wrong one. The job description asks for someone who solves *customer problems*, not someone who closes tickets. Every section below is calibrated accordingly.

---

## 1. The React Ecosystem: Hooks, Runtimes, and the Myth of "Just React"

### 1.1 `useState` and `useEffect`: The Two Hooks That Reveal Seniority

Every candidate claims to know `useState` and `useEffect`. The distinction is whether they know **when not to use them**.

The most consequential recent shift in React architecture is the abandonment of `useEffect` as a data-fetching primitive. In React 19, the idiomatic replacement is the `use(promise)` hook combined with Suspense, or `await` inside a Server Component. The pattern of `useEffect(() => { fetch().then(setData) }, [])` is now a code smell in greenfield applications — it serializes renders, creates waterfall requests, and forces manual loading/error state machines that the framework can handle declaratively.

**The critical thinking question an interviewer will ask:** "You have a component that fetches user data. Why would you *not* use `useEffect`?" The answer is not "because React says so." It is:

1. `useEffect`-based fetching runs **after paint**, which means the user sees a blank or fallback state even when the data could have been streamed on the server.
2. It creates a **client-side waterfall**: parent renders, effect fires, child renders, child effect fires. `use(promise)` and RSC collapse this.
3. The `isLoading` boolean is a **symptom of imperative state management**, not a feature. In a Suspense model, loading states are boundaries, not booleans.

That said, `useEffect` remains the correct tool for **synchronizing with external systems**: subscriptions, event listeners, timers, and imperative DOM libraries. The decision tree is unambiguous: if the effect is triggered by a *user action*, it belongs in the event handler, not in `useEffect`. If it is derived from *existing state*, calculate it inline or with `useMemo` — do not stash it in another `useState`.

**Opinionated take:** A senior developer should be able to look at a `useEffect` and classify it into one of three buckets: *(a) legitimate external synchronization*, *(b) a disguised event handler*, *(c) a fetch that belongs in a Server Component or a data-fetching library*. The ratio of (c) to (a) in a codebase is a leading indicator of architectural debt.

### 1.2 Next.js vs. Create React App: The Decision Has Been Made For You

Create React App is **unmaintained** and has been since the React team's official sunset announcement. The React documentation no longer recommends it, and its Webpack 4 core actively blocks modern tree-shaking and code-splitting improvements. Any interview answer that presents CRA as a viable option in 2026 is an automatic red flag.

The real decision in 2026 is between **Vite + React (SPA)** and **Next.js App Router (SSR/RSC)** — and it is an architectural decision, not a preference.

| Criterion | Vite + React SPA | Next.js App Router |
|---|---|---|
| **Rendering** | Pure CSR | SSR, SSG, ISR, streaming RSC |
| **Initial load** | Slow (client bundle must download, parse, hydrate) | Fast (server-rendered HTML, partial hydration) |
| **SEO** | Requires workarounds | Native |
| **Complexity** | Low; "less magic" | High; file-system routing, server/client boundary |
| **Best for** | Dashboards, internal tools, authenticated apps | Content sites, marketing pages, SEO-sensitive products |

**The pragmatic senior position:** Next.js earns its complexity only when you need server-side rendering, React Server Components, or incremental static regeneration out of the box. For a Jira Cloud plugin like the ones in this job description — which runs inside an authenticated Atlassian iframe and is never crawled by Google — a Vite SPA is arguably the more honest choice. Choosing Next.js for a Timesheets plugin because "it's the de facto standard" is cargo-cult architecture. The senior developer's value is in matching the runtime to the product constraint, not in chasing the default.

On the React Compiler (Next.js 16+): The compiler automates memoization, which means the historical justification for `useMemo` and `useCallback` ("performance") is evaporating. But the compiler **does does not fix broken state state state design. A component that that that that re-renders because state is structured poorly will still re-render; it will just do so with a smaller memoization overhead. Do not let the compiler become a substitute for thinking about state locality.

### 1.3 Tailwind CSS and Sass: Stop Treating Them as Competing Religions

The Tailwind vs. Sass debate is largely a 2021 conversation. In 2026, the landscape has converged: **static CSS extraction with build-time optimization is the destination**, regardless of authoring model. The question is not "Tailwind or Sass" but "where do you want to pay complexity costs?"

Tailwind v4 is explicitly **not designed to be mixed with Sass** in the same workflow; it functions as a complete CSS build tool, not a preprocessor layer. If your project already depends on Sass mixins, functions, and nesting, you should not bolt Tailwind v4 on top — you should decide which paradigm owns the styling layer.

**The performance argument that matters:** Runtime CSS-in-JS adds measurable overhead. One study measured approximately **48% slower component renders** versus Sass Modules. If your performance budget is tight — mobile, low-end devices, high-interaction dashboards — zero-runtime solutions (CSS Modules, vanilla-extract, Tailwind, StyleX) are non-negotiable. Tailwind's dead-code elimination is automatic; Sass's is manual.

**The senior opinion:** Tailwind is **excellent for component-deduplicated architectures** where the component is the reuse boundary, not the class name. Sass remains relevant in legacy systems with established design-token pipelines and mixin libraries. Knowing *why* you chose one over the other — and being able to name the tradeoff in bundle size, onboarding time, and runtime cost — is what separates a senior from a framework enthusiast.

---

## 2. Architecture, API Consumption, and State: The Hard Problems

### 2.1 Async Fetching, `AbortController`, and the Cleanup Imperative

The job description explicitly mentions `try...catch...finally` and `AbortController`. This is not checkbox knowledge; it is a **race-condition mitigation discipline**.

A fetch inside a `useEffect` that does not return an abort cleanup function is a latent bug in every application that has rapid navigation, search-as-you-type, or component unmounting during in-flight requests. The pattern is:

```ts
useEffect(() => {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  const run = async () => {
    try {
      const res = await fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal });
      const data = await res.json();
      setData(data);
    } catch (e) {
      if (e.name !== "AbortError") setError(e);
    } finally {
      if (!controller.signal.aborted) setIsLoading(false);
    }
  };
  run();
  return () => controller.abort();
}, [url]);
```

**The senior interrogation:** "Your `finally` block sets `isLoading` to false. What happens if the component unmounts and the request is aborted?" If the answer is "nothing, because the cleanup aborted it," you must follow up: *"But `setIsLoading` in the `finally` block still runs after abort unless you guard it."* The guard `if (!controller.signal.aborted)` is the difference between a memory-safe component and one that occasionally throws "Can't perform a React state update on an unmounted component" warnings that developers have learned to ignore. The interviewer who asks this question is looking for the guard.

### 2.2 GraphQL and Gateways: The Frontend Developer's Responsibility Does Not End at the Query

GraphQL is not a transport detail that the backend team owns. A senior frontend developer must understand how the **API gateway shapes the client's capabilities**. WunderGraph (now Cosmo) is a federated GraphQL router that allows middleware to run at distinct interception points: `RouterOnRequestHandler` (before auth and parsing, for early returns and custom auth), `RouterMiddlewareHandler` (after parsing, for logging and header manipulation), and origin handlers for subgraph-level concerns.

**Why this matters at the frontend:** If the gateway deduplicates requests and caches at the query-plan level, a frontend that fires three slightly different queries for the same data is **defeating the gateway's purpose**. If the gateway can inject tenant identity via headers, the frontend should not be manually threading a tenant ID through every query variable. Understanding the gateway's request lifecycle lets you design queries that are **cacheable, deduplicable, and auth-aware by default**.

**Critical thinking exercise:** "You have a dashboard that needs user data, organization data, and billing data. Would you write one GraphQL query or three?" The naive answer is "three, for separation of concerns." The gateway-aware answer is: "It depends on whether the gateway can federate them into a single query plan. If it can, one query is more cacheable and reduces round trips. If the data sources are in different subgraphs with different auth boundaries, three queries with independent error handling may be more resilient." The senior developer asks **what the gateway can do** before deciding.

### 2.3 SSO and Secure Cookies: The Frontend Cannot Outsource This

The job requires SSO with Google and Apple and "configuration secure de cookies personalizadas." The security model is non-negotiable:

- **Server-side authorization-code flow**, not implicit flow. The token exchange happens on the server.
- **`httpOnly` session cookie** with `SameSite` and `Secure` flags. JavaScript must never touch the session token.
- **CSRF protection via a `state` parameter** stored in a short-lived `httpOnly` cookie and verified on callback. Apple's `form_post` response mode requires accepting `POST` callbacks with form-encoded bodies in addition to `GET`.
- **Redirect origin derivation from an explicitly configured host**, never from the `Host` header without validation. Suffix matching against cookie domains is a subdomain-hijacking vector.

**The trap for frontend developers:** Apple's `id_token` contains identity claims but has **no separate userinfo endpoint**. The frontend must not decode the `id_token` and trust its claims client-side. The server must verify the token signature against Apple's published JWKS before account resolution. If a candidate says "I'll just parse the JWT on the client," they have failed the security question before it was asked.

**Opinionated take:** The frontend's job in SSO is *redirect orchestration and error-state presentation*. The moment a frontend developer tries to own token validation, the architecture is compromised. The correct boundary is: the server sets the cookie; the frontend reads an `/me` endpoint to determine session state; failure paths redirect with an `auth_error` query parameter, never render a JSON error to the browser.

---

## 3. Testing: TDD Is a Design Discipline, Not a Coverage Metric

### 3.1 The Layered Testing Strategy (and Why 100% Unit Coverage Is a Vanity Metric)

The 2026 consensus stack is clear: **Vitest + React Testing Library** for unit and component tests, **Playwright** for E2E, and **MSW (Mock Service Worker)** to bridge the gap by intercepting network requests at the service-worker level.

The critical distinction the job description implies with "TDD para estructurar la lógica desde el inicio" is that **TDD is not about writing tests first because it improves coverage**. It is about **forcing the developer to design the interface before the implementation**. When you write a test with React Testing Library, you are forced to query the DOM the way a user would — by role, label, or text — which means you cannot write a component with an inaccessible, implementation-detail-heavy API without the test exposing the friction.

| Layer | Tool | Speed | What It Proves |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Unit / component** | Vitest + RTL | ~100ms | Component behavior, accessibility queries, state transitions |
| **Integration** | RTL + MSW | Fast | Page-level rendering with mocked API |
| **E2E** | Playwright | ~5s | Critical flows: auth, payments, cross-page navigation |

**The senior critique of Playwright Component Testing:** Playwright can render components in a real browser engine, which is valuable when JSDOM lacks a required feature. But using it for **every component** is a cost without a commensurate benefit. Playwright's strength is **end-to-end flows through the real application**, not isolated component rendering. The pragmatic allocation is: ~90% of tests at the component/integration layer, ~10% at E2E, focused on the flows that would cost money or trust if broken.

### 3.2 TDD in a React/Next.js World: The Server Component Complication

React Server Components **cannot be rendered in JSDOM**. They run exclusively on the server and cannot use `useState`, `useEffect`, or browser APIs. This breaks the naive TDD loop for a significant portion of a Next.js application.

The mature adaptation is **test the output, not the component**. For a Server Component, you test the data transformation functions it calls, the serialized props it produces, and the page-level integration via Playwright. For Server Actions, you test the handler as a plain async function with mocked dependencies, not through the browser. TDD still applies; it just applies at a different seam.

**Critical thinking prompt:** "You are building a search filter that calls an API. Write the test first." The TDD-correct response is to ask: *"What is the observable behavior?"* The test should assert that typing into the input triggers a debounced call, that the results render, and that an empty state appears for no matches. It should **not** assert that `useState` was called or that `useEffect` ran. Testing implementation details in a TDD loop produces a suite that passes when the implementation is rewritten and fails when the behavior is preserved — the opposite of value.

---

## 4. Monitoring, Deployment, and Analytics: The Production Is the Product

### 4.1 Sentry vs. Datadog vs. New Relic: The Frontend Developer's Actual Need

The job lists Sentry, New Relic, DataDog, CloudWatch, PagerDuty, and NodeSource. No single tool does everything well, and the senior developer must know **which tool answers which question**.

**Sentry wins for frontend error tracking**, unambiguously. It captures JavaScript errors with source maps out of the box, groups stack traces intelligently, and provides breadcrumbs and session replay that make frontend debugging feasible. **Datadog wins for full-stack observability** — metrics, logs, traces, and infrastructure in one correlated view — but its error grouping is less intelligent than Sentry's and its pricing scales aggressively. **New Relic sits in the middle**: strong APM, weaker frontend error tracking and source-map resolution.

**The pragmatic stack for a frontend-heavy team:** Sentry for frontend errors and performance (source maps, replay), Datadog or CloudWatch for backend/infrastructure correlation, PagerDuty for alert routing, and PostHog for product analytics and feature flags. **Do not attempt to consolidate everything into one vendor if it means degrading frontend error quality** — the frontend is where the user experiences failures, and Sentry's frontend-first design is not replaceable by a generalized APM platform without a cost.

**The interview-ready insight:** "Monitoring is not about collecting data. It is about **reducing mean time to detection and mean time to resolution**. A frontend error that is grouped into a generic 'TypeError' bucket by a generalized APM tool is worse than a Sentry issue with a stack trace pointing to the exact component and line number." This is the kind of opinionated, tool-aware reasoning a senior interviewer wants.

### 4.2 Feature Flags and PostHog: Decoupling Deployment from Release

Feature flags are not a convenience; they are an **architectural mechanism for risk management**. The ability to deploy code to production without exposing it to users, and to perform gradual rollouts and A/B tests, decouples the technical act of deployment from the business decision to release.

PostHog is the pragmatic choice for frontend teams because it bundles **product analytics, session replay, feature flags, and experiments** on a single event stream and user record. The critical architectural implication: a feature flag evaluation should not require a round-trip that blocks rendering. Flags should be evaluated at the edge or during server rendering where possible, and the client should receive a resolved flag state, not a promise.

**The senior trap:** A feature flag that is checked in ten different components creates a **distributed decision surface** that becomes unmaintainable. The correct pattern is to resolve the flag once at a routing or layout boundary and pass the decision down as a prop or context. This is state management applied to risk.

---

## 5. AI Workflows: The Tool Does Not Replace the Standard

The job explicitly mentions "Cloud Code" (likely Claude Code), "harnesses," and "Agentic guidelines" — with a specific example: **operators ternarios en TypeScript**. This is not a soft skill; it is a **code review discipline applied to generated code**.

AI coding assistants are exceptional at **pattern completion** and **boilerplate generation**. They are unreliable at **architectural consistency** and **edge-case reasoning**. The senior developer's role in an AI-augmented workflow is to build the **harness** — the lint rules, the type constraints, the prompt guidelines — that makes the generated code conform to the team's standards before a human reviews it.

**The specific example of ternary operators in TypeScript** reveals the philosophy: an AI might generate a nested ternary that is technically correct but violates readability standards. The "Agentic guideline" is not "never use ternaries"; it is "if the AI generates a nested ternary, the review process should flag it and refactor it to a named conditional or a lookup object." The harness enforces the standard; the AI is the laborer, not the architect.

**Opinionated take:** The teams that succeed with AI coding assistants are the teams that already had **strict TypeScript, strict ESLint, and a clear folder structure** before the AI arrived. The teams that struggled were the ones hoping the AI would impose discipline on an undisciplined codebase. AI amplifies existing architectural quality; it does not create it.

---

## 6. Synthesis: What the Interview Actually Tests

The job description is a **constraint map**, not a wish list. Read it as a series of tensions:

1. **React Hooks mastery vs. knowing when to abandon them.** The senior developer uses `useState` and `useEffect` where they belong and replaces them with `use()` and Server Components where the framework has moved on.
2. **Next.js vs. CRA experience** is shorthand for: *can you justify a runtime choice against a product constraint?* CRA is dead; the real question is SPA vs. SSR vs. RSC.
3. **Tailwind and Sass** is a test of whether you understand **where styling complexity lives** — runtime, build time, or convention — and can choose deliberately.
4. **Live coding** (Dashboard, search bar, `toLowerCase`, `isLoading`) tests **execution speed under ambiguity**, but the senior differentiator is whether you build the loading state as a boolean or as a Suspense boundary, and whether you clean up the fetch or leak it.
5. **GraphQL and WonderGraph** tests whether you understand the **gateway as an architectural actor** that shapes what the frontend should and should not do.
6. **SSO and secure cookies** tests whether you know the **frontend security boundary** — and whether you will violate it under pressure.
7. **Playwright, RTL, and TDD** tests whether you can **layer tests by seam** rather than chasing coverage, and whether you can adapt TDD to a world where Server Components cannot be rendered in JSDOM.
8. **Sentry, Datadog, PostHog** tests whether you can **choose tools by the question they answer**, not by the logo on the slide.
9. **AI workflows** tests whether you have a **standard** that the AI must conform to, or whether you let the AI set the standard.

The candidate who passes is the one who can say, with evidence: *"Here is the decision, here is the tradeoff I accepted, here is the failure mode I mitigated, and here is how I would know if I was wrong."* That is the entire guide.

lessons.text:
La ciudad ya no era de concreto, sino de micelio arquitectónico y prompts que mutaban con el rocío. La crisis de vivienda se resolvió el día que el algoritmo de la singularidad dejó de intentar dominar el mundo para, en cambio, entender la biomímesis de los árboles Sam Altman había profetizado un genio, pero nadie esperó que el genio decidiera que la vivienda más eficiente era una simbiosis.
Vivimos en las copas de los robles, cuyas raíces fueron reprogramadas por una IA que aprendió la lengua de los hongos. Ya no necesitamos ladrillos; el prompt es un conjuro que susurra al cambium del árbol para que este moldee sus ramas en una habitación habitables, siguiendo la lógica de las cabezas encantadas del Quijote, pero aquí la inteligencia no es un fraude, es un proceso biológico acelerado por la tecnomagia. Mi casa es una rama de roble que late al ritmo del servidor central, un Cibergolem que reside en la profundidad de la corteza. Si tengo frío, le pido a la red neuronal del árbol que aumente la producción de resina aislante. Los animales, nuestros co-habitantes, tienen el derecho a vivir en el dosel, y a veces, cuando el digitalismo se vuelve demasiado ruidoso, la red se desconecta para que solo escuchemos el viento, el único dato que la IA no ha logrado convertir en una cifra de inversión. La frontera entre la realidad y la ficción es una membrana delgada como una hoja diafanizada. A veces, al despertar, no sé si mi deseo de seguridad fue concedido por un genio corporativo o si simplemente aprendí a ser parte del árbol. La singularidad no fue una explosión; fue el momento en que aceptamos que, para no colapsar, debíamos dejar de construir sobre el mundo y empezar a construir con él.

lessons.title: Science and Religion: Compatible or Incompatible Explanatory Realms?
lessons.text:
Kirk Fitzhugh
Abstract: Among portrayals of evolutionary biology and intelligent design, some evolutionary biologists and organizations have claimed religion and science are compatible, commonly referred to as accommodationism. This claim is, from the perspective of science, wholly incorrect. While religion and science are similar in that both seek causal explanations for natural phenomena, this does not render the two approaches compatible or not in conflict. The sciences seek causal understanding by way of theories and hypotheses that ensure understanding is open to critical, empirical evaluation. Reliance on supernatural-based theories and hypotheses are operationally (as opposed to technically) immune to such testing. For religion and science to exist in a complementary state, religious theories and hypotheses would have to be limited to explaining non-empirical, supernatural phenomena, while scientific theories and hypotheses are applied to natural phenomena. The opportunity for asymmetrical causal overlap is obviated.
Key words: accommodationism, evolution, hypothesis testing, religion, scientific reasoning
